question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+yz$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨1,2,3⟩$ and $b=⟨2,3,4⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+yz$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨1,2,3⟩$ and $b=⟨2,3,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,3,4)-f(1,2,3) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,3,4⟩-⟨1,2,3⟩) \\ 20-8 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 12 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨4x,z,y⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨4{c}_{1},{c}_{3},{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 12 & =⟨4{c}_{1},{c}_{3},{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 12 & =4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-3}{1} \\ x-1 & =y-2=z-3\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t+1,\,y=t+2,\,z=t+3,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t+1,\,{c}_{2}=t+2,\,{c}_{3}=t+3.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $12=4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(t+1)+(t+2)+(t+3) & =12 \\ 4t+4+t+2+t+3 & =12 \\ 6t+9 & =12 \\ 6t & =3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+2=\frac{5}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}+3=\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2},\frac{7}{2}).$
